title: Fatty Liver Disease Now Affects One in Three Adults Worldwide — and Most Don't Know It
excerpt: The silent epidemic of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease is surging globally, with India among the hardest-hit countries. New treatments and screening tools offer hope, but experts warn early detection remains critically low.
body:
• An estimated 32% of adults globally now have metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly known as NAFLD, making it the most common chronic liver disease worldwide.
  • In India, roughly one in three adults and children have fatty liver disease, with prevalence reaching 38.6% in adults and even higher rates among those with diabetes or obesity.
  • Resmetirom (Rezdiffra), approved by the FDA in March 2024 and in the EU in August 2025, is the first drug specifically targeting MASH — the severe inflammatory stage — and has shown the ability to reverse liver fibrosis.
  • Fewer than 3% of people with MASLD know they have the condition. Experts say routine screening with simple blood tests and ultrasound could prevent progression to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

A disease that most people have never heard of now affects more than one in three adults on the planet, and the majority of them have no idea. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease — MASLD, formerly called non-alcoholic fatty liver disease or NAFLD — has quietly become the world's most common chronic liver condition, driven by rising rates of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and sedentary lifestyles.

According to a 2026 review published in Diabetologia, the estimated global prevalence stands at 32.4%, with approximately 46.9 new cases per 1,000 person-years. The Asia Pacific region bears a disproportionate share: more than half of the world's estimated MASLD cases are concentrated there, where roughly 60% of the global population lives. Prevalence in the region has jumped by over 50% in the past two decades.

India's Outsized Burden

India faces a particularly acute challenge. A systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Journal of Clinical and Experimental Hepatology by researchers at AIIMS New Delhi and SGPGIMS Lucknow found that the pooled prevalence of NAFLD among Indian adults was 38.6%. Among high-risk groups — those with diabetes, obesity, or metabolic syndrome — the figure climbed to 52.8%. Even in rural communities, prevalence reached 28% to 31%, demolishing the assumption that fatty liver is a disease of urban, affluent populations.

"Available data suggest that approximately one in three adults or children have NAFLD in India," the study's authors concluded. They noted that with India's diabetes prevalence now between 15% and 19% and metabolic syndrome affecting roughly 30% of adults, the burden is set to grow further.

A Disease That Progresses in Silence

What makes MASLD particularly dangerous is its stealth. The disease begins with fat accumulation in the liver — often entirely asymptomatic — but can progress through inflammation (MASH), fibrosis, cirrhosis, and eventually liver cancer or liver failure. A Diabetologia review noted that roughly one-third of MASLD patients develop inflammatory steatohepatitis or significant fibrosis within ten years, with faster progression in individuals with obesity and diabetes.

Awareness is alarmingly low on both sides of the stethoscope. A global survey found that fewer than 3% of people living with MASLD were aware of their diagnosis. In Australia, only about 40% of primary care physicians could accurately identify high-risk patients. In Southeast Asia, 79% of healthcare providers reported inadequate training in obesity management and lifestyle counselling related to liver disease.

"Fibrosis is a precancerous condition and the most common indication for a liver transplant in the next 10 years."

— Martina Müller-Schilling, MD, University Hospital Regensburg

New Drugs Change the Treatment Landscape

For decades, the only prescription for fatty liver disease was lifestyle modification: lose weight, eat better, exercise more. That changed in March 2024 when the US Food and Drug Administration approved resmetirom (Rezdiffra), a thyroid hormone receptor beta agonist, for adults with non-cirrhotic MASH and moderate to advanced fibrosis. The European Union followed with its own approval in August 2025.

In the Phase III MAESTRO-NASH trial, a majority of participants who took resmetirom saw their liver fibrosis either reversed or halted. The drug also reduced hepatic fat content, liver stiffness, and serum lipid levels.

"Until now, liver disease has never had a treatment shown to reverse fibrosis, which is the damage from which all other issues stem."

— Mary Rinella, MD, Director of Metabolic and Fatty Liver Disease, UChicago Medicine

GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide are also being used in clinical obesity management and have shown benefits for liver fat reduction. Several other drugs — including FGF21 analogues and pan-PPAR agonists — are in Phase III trials.

Screening Could Save Lives

Experts say the key to reducing MASLD's toll lies in early detection. In primary care, initial screening can include a combination of ultrasound and liver enzyme blood tests. For patients with cardiometabolic risk factors, the Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) blood test and enhanced liver fibrosis test can help determine the severity of scarring. A three-parameter biomarker panel published in Cell Metabolism was able to distinguish MASH patients from those with simple fatty liver with a specificity of 90%.

Yet no country has implemented a comprehensive MASLD public health response. A study of 102 nations found zero had dedicated strategic documentation for the disease. The WHO's own guidance and action plan documents still do not address MASLD.

What the Diaspora Should Know

For Indians living abroad, the risk profile is compounded by genetic susceptibility. South Asian populations carry higher rates of insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome at lower body mass indices than Western populations, meaning fatty liver can develop even without visible obesity. The PNPLA3 gene variant associated with accelerated liver fat accumulation is more prevalent in Asian populations.

Physicians recommend that adults with any cardiometabolic risk factor — diabetes, hypertension, obesity, or high triglycerides — ask their doctor about liver screening, even in the absence of symptoms. Lifestyle interventions remain the first line of defence: studies show that reducing caloric intake by 500 calories per day can improve fibrosis, and high-intensity interval exercise may be more effective than weight loss alone.

In September 2025, the United Nations included MASLD in the political declaration of its fourth high-level meeting on non-communicable diseases — a significant milestone, though experts argue the disease still needs to be elevated to high-priority status to unlock the funding and policy attention it demands.
